64.title: Rachel dies on the road (Genesis 35:16–20)
64.hook: she dies bearing Benjamin and is buried by the roadside; tradition says she still weeps for her children
64.howItsDone: Many Jews visit Rachel's Tomb near Bethlehem to pray, especially for children and for the health of family, and Jeremiah's words about Rachel weeping are read in synagogue on the second day of Rosh Hashanah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dinah: a hard chapter, told without softening, where the one it happened to never speaks. Your line: not every story ends well. Today a new part of the path begins, and it starts with a mother.

The family is traveling south, toward Bethlehem, and Rachel is pregnant again. Rachel: the one Jacob loved at first sight by the well, and worked seven years for, then seven more. She waited years for a child, at last had Joseph, and named him with a hope: may God add another son. Now the hope is coming true. And the labor is hard. Very hard. The midwife tries to comfort her: don't be afraid, this one is a son too.
screen: `THE ONE JACOB LOVED AT THE WELL.` → `MAY GOD ADD ANOTHER SON.` → `A HARD LABOR ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: As she is dying, Rachel names the baby Ben-oni: son of my sorrow. Jacob gives him another name: Binyamin, Benjamin, son of the right hand. One name remembers the pain; the other chooses strength. Then the Torah says, simply: "And Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath—the same is Beth-lehem." In the way. Not in the family tomb at Hebron, where Abraham and Sarah lie, where Leah will lie, where Jacob himself will be buried. Rachel is buried beside the road, and Jacob sets up a pillar on her grave. Why there? Centuries later, the prophet Jeremiah hears a sound on that road, as the people are being led away into exile: "Rachel weeping for her children." She refuses to be comforted, the verse says, because her children are gone. And God answers her: refrain your voice from weeping; your children will come back. The rabbis put these together. Rashi, the great medieval commentator, passes on a midrash: Jacob buried Rachel by the road on purpose, so that when her children were driven into exile along it, she would be there to cry for them, and her crying would be heard. Rachel became the mother who never stops praying for her kids. And not only in books. Her tomb, near Bethlehem, is still visited today. People pray there, especially people longing for a child, or worried about one. A woman who waited so long to be a mother became, in Jewish memory, the mother of everyone far from home.

65.title: The coat (Genesis 37:1–11)
65.hook: a favorite son, a special coat, and dreams of sheaves bowing down
65.howItsDone: The Joseph story is read in synagogue over several weekly portions in the winter, and the Talmud's lesson from the coat (Shabbat 10b) is a classic text on treating children evenly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ben-oni: Rachel's son of sorrow, and a mother buried where her children would pass. Your line: she weeps for her children. Today, her firstborn.

The later curfew. The bigger photo on the fridge. In some homes, a favorite child is the thing nobody says out loud. In Jacob's house, nobody even pretends. Joseph is seventeen, Rachel's son, and Rachel is gone. He tends the flocks with his older brothers and brings back bad reports about some of them to their father. Then one day Jacob gives Joseph a gift. Only Joseph. Something the brothers see every single day.
screen: `THE BIGGER PHOTO ON THE FRIDGE.` → `JOSEPH, SEVENTEEN, RACHEL'S SON.` → `A GIFT FOR ONLY ONE.`

segments.voice: The Torah says it straight out: "Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age; and he made him a coat of many colours." Many colors is how the old translations put it, and the musical too. But nobody is sure what the Hebrew means. The words are ketonet passim. Ketonet is a tunic. Passim is the puzzle. Many colors is one old guess. Others think it means long sleeves, reaching to the palms and the ankles: a coat for someone who doesn't have to work in the fields. The phrase turns up again in the book of Samuel, worn by a king's daughter. Whatever it looked like, the brothers understood it perfectly. They hated him, the text says, and couldn't speak a peaceful word to him. Then Joseph has dreams, and tells them. Sheaves of grain in a field, and all the brothers' sheaves bow down to his. Then the sun, the moon and eleven stars bow down to him. Even Jacob scolds him for that one, but the text says his father kept the saying in mind. The Talmud draws a lesson from the coat. Never favor one child over the others, it says: for a little bit of fine wool that Jacob gave Joseph beyond his brothers, they grew jealous, and in the end our ancestors went down into Egypt. The whole story of slavery in Egypt, the Talmud says, begins with a coat.

66.title: Into the pit (Genesis 37:12–36)
66.hook: the brothers throw Joseph in a pit and sell him; Reuben comes back too late
66.howItsDone: Some Jewish teachers use Reuben's delay to talk about acting on a good impulse right away, echoing the saying in Pirkei Avot, if not now, when?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the coat: a gift for the favorite son, and dreams of sheaves bowing down. Your line: favorites cost. Today we find out how much.

The brothers are far from home, pasturing the flocks, when Jacob sends Joseph to check on them. From a long way off, they see him coming. Maybe it's the coat they recognize first. They say to each other: "Behold, this dreamer cometh." Let's kill him, throw him in a pit, and say a wild animal ate him. Then we'll see what becomes of his dreams. Out in the fields, with no father watching, a family grudge turns into a plan.
screen: `THEY SEE HIM FROM FAR OFF.` → `THIS DREAMER COMETH.` → `A GRUDGE BECOMES A PLAN.`

segments.voice: Reuben, the oldest, speaks up. Don't kill him; just throw him into this pit. The Torah tells us his secret plan: come back later, pull Joseph out, and bring him home to their father. So they strip off the coat and throw Joseph in, and the text adds a detail: "the pit was empty, there was no water in it." Then, while Joseph is down there, they sit down to eat bread. A caravan passes, traders going down to Egypt. Judah has an idea: what do we gain by killing him? Let's sell him. And Joseph is sold for twenty pieces of silver. The text gets a little tangled here about who pulled him out and who sold him, and readers still puzzle over it. And Reuben? Somewhere else. He comes back to the pit, and it's empty. He tears his clothes: "The child is not; and as for me, whither shall I go?" The midrash has a sharp line about this. Had Reuben known that the Torah would write down that he tried to save Joseph, it says, he would have picked him up on his shoulders and carried him home to his father right then. The good intention was real. The delay cost everything. Then the brothers dip the coat in goat's blood and bring it to Jacob, and he says, "an evil beast hath devoured him." He tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, and refuses to be comforted.

67.title: Judah and Tamar (Genesis 38)
67.hook: shown his own seal, Judah says "She is more righteous than I"
67.howItsDone: Jewish tradition draws from Tamar the teaching that publicly shaming another person is gravely wrong, and honors Judah's admission as a model of owning a mistake; Tamar's son Perez is remembered as an ancestor of King David.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bor, the empty pit: Joseph sold, and Reuben back too late. Your line: don't come back too late. Today, Judah, the brother who said sell him.

Right in the middle of Joseph's story, just as he's dragged off to Egypt, the Torah cuts away, like a TV show that suddenly spends a whole episode on a side character. The side character is Judah. His oldest son marries a woman named Tamar, and dies. By the custom of the time, the next son should give her a child in his brother's name. He refuses, and dies too. Judah has one son left, and he's afraid. So he sends Tamar back to her father's house: wait until my youngest grows up. Then he never sends for her. Tamar is left waiting, a widow with no future.
screen: `THE STORY CUTS AWAY TO JUDAH.` → `TAMAR, TWICE A WIDOW.` → `SENT HOME TO WAIT, AND FORGOTTEN.`

segments.voice: Years pass. Tamar hears that Judah is coming through on the way to shear his sheep. She takes off her widow's clothes, covers her face with a veil, and sits by the road. Judah doesn't recognize her; he thinks she's a woman for hire. He has nothing to pay with, so she asks for a pledge: your seal, your cord, and your staff. His ID card, basically. Three months later, word comes: Tamar is pregnant. Judah, the head of the family, gives the sentence: bring her out and let her be burned. As she's being brought out, Tamar sends a message. Not an accusation. She doesn't say, it was you. She sends the seal, the cord and the staff: the man who owns these is the father. Please look, whose are these? That word, look, recognize, is the same Hebrew the brothers used when they handed Jacob the bloody coat: look, is this your son's? That time they asked their father to recognize a lie, and a midrash puts those words in Judah's mouth. Now Judah is asked to recognize something true. And he does: "She is more righteous than I." The Talmud notices how Tamar did it. She was ready to die rather than shame him in public; she gave him the chance to admit it himself. Tamar has twins, Perez and Zerah. And from Perez, the book of Ruth tells us, comes King David.

68.title: Potiphar's house (Genesis 39)
68.hook: Joseph rises, is falsely accused, and lands in prison
68.howItsDone: Jewish tradition calls Joseph Yosef ha-Tzaddik, Joseph the righteous, and rabbinic teaching ties the title to how he acted in Potiphar's house.

segments.voice: Yesterday, haker na: a seal, a cord, a staff, and a man who finally said she is more righteous than I. Your line: she was right. Now, back to Joseph, a slave in Egypt.

Joseph is up for sale again. Not long ago he was the favorite son with the fancy coat. Since then he's been thrown in a pit by his own brothers, sold to strangers, carried down to Egypt, and sold again, far from everyone he knows. An Egyptian official named Potiphar, captain of Pharaoh's guard, buys him. Joseph has every reason to shut down. To do the minimum. To be bitter for the rest of his life.
screen: `FAVORITE SON TO SLAVE.` → `SOLD TO POTIPHAR.` → `EVERY REASON TO SHUT DOWN.`

segments.voice: The chapter opens with a line that becomes its drumbeat: "And the LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man." Joseph works, and everything he touches goes well. Potiphar notices, and soon puts him in charge of the whole house. Then, trouble. Potiphar's wife wants Joseph, and asks him, day after day. He refuses, and his answer is about loyalty and about God: his master trusted him with everything, so "how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" One day, when the house is empty, she grabs his garment. He runs, and leaves it in her hand. And she uses it. She tells the household, then her husband, that the Hebrew slave attacked her, and holds up the garment as proof. Notice: this is the second time a piece of Joseph's clothing is used to tell a lie about him. First the coat, dipped in blood. Now this. So Joseph, who did the right thing, lands in prison. And here's the part that makes the chapter: the same line comes back. The LORD was with Joseph. In prison. The keeper of the prison notices him, and soon Joseph is running the place, looking after the other prisoners. Nothing in the story says the pit or the prison was good. What it says is that Joseph kept being Joseph wherever they put him. Honest in the good house. Useful in the bad one.

69.title: Dreams in prison (Genesis 40)
69.hook: the butler and the baker; the butler forgets him
69.howItsDone: Jewish tradition calls gratitude hakarat ha-tov, recognizing the good, and teaches that forgetting a kindness done to you is a real failing; the butler is the classic example.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Potiphar's house: falsely accused, sent to prison, and still the LORD was with Joseph. Your line: good in the pit too.

I'll put in a word for you. I'll send your résumé along. I won't forget this. Everyone has had a friend who promised, and then, nothing. Not cruelty. They just got busy with their own good news. In Joseph's prison, two new men arrive from Pharaoh's own household: the chief butler, who pours Pharaoh's wine, and the chief baker. Both have fallen out of favor. One morning Joseph, who is looking after them, notices that they both look miserable.
screen: `I WON'T FORGET THIS.` → `THE BUTLER AND THE BAKER.` → `TWO SAD FACES IN THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: Start with what Joseph does first. He notices. A prisoner himself, falsely accused, he still looks at the faces around him and asks, why do you look so sad today? We each had a dream, they say, and there's nobody to interpret it. Joseph answers: "Do not interpretations belong to God?" Tell me. The butler dreams of a vine with three branches; the grapes ripen, and he squeezes them into Pharaoh's cup. Joseph says: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and give you your job back. Then he asks for one thing. Remember me when it goes well for you. Mention me to Pharaoh. I was stolen from my land, and here too I've done nothing to deserve this dungeon. The baker, encouraged, tells his dream: three baskets of bread on his head, and birds eating from the top one. Joseph's answer is grim: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head too, but off of you. Three days later, on Pharaoh's birthday, it all happens exactly as Joseph said. Then the chapter ends with one of the loneliest verses in the Torah: "Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgot him." It says it twice, remember and forget, as if to let it sink in. Two more full years go by. A midrash reads those two years as a lesson for Joseph himself, about putting too much hope in a man. But you can read the verse the other way too: as a lesson for the butler, and for anyone who ever got out and left someone behind.

70.title: Pharaoh's dreams (Genesis 41)
70.hook: seven fat cows, seven thin ones, and a plan to store grain
70.howItsDone: Jews read this chapter in the weekly Torah portion Miketz, which the calendar often places during Hanukkah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dreams in prison: the butler got out and forgot. Your line: don't forget Joseph. It's the end of a week that began with Rachel's grave and ran through a coat, a pit, Tamar, Potiphar's house and a prison. Today, the door opens.

Two full years after the butler forgot, Pharaoh has a nightmare. He's standing by the Nile, and seven cows come up out of the river, sleek and fat, and graze in the reeds. Then seven more come up, thin and ugly, and eat the seven fat cows. And they're still just as thin. Pharaoh wakes, falls back asleep, and dreams again: seven full ears of grain on one stalk, swallowed by seven thin, scorched ones. All the wise men of Egypt are called. Nobody can explain it. And suddenly the butler, standing right there, remembers something.
screen: `SEVEN FAT COWS, SEVEN THIN.` → `NOBODY CAN EXPLAIN IT.` → `THE BUTLER REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: They rush Joseph out of the dungeon. He shaves and changes his clothes, another change of garment in this story, and stands before Pharaoh. I hear you can interpret dreams, says the king. Joseph's first words: "It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace." Not me. God. The two dreams are one, he explains. Seven good years are coming, years of plenty across Egypt. Then seven years of famine, so heavy that the plenty will be forgotten. The dream came twice because it's certain, and soon. But Joseph doesn't stop at explaining. He gives Pharaoh a plan: find a wise man, collect a fifth of the harvest in the good years, store the grain in the cities, and when the famine comes, the country won't perish. Pharaoh looks around: who could be wiser than the man who just said this? Joseph goes from the prison to the palace, second only to Pharaoh. He's thirty years old. He was seventeen in the pit. He gets a ring, fine linen, a gold chain, an Egyptian name, and a wife. His two sons' names tell you what's inside him. Manasseh: God made me forget my hardship and my father's house. Ephraim: God made me fruitful in the land of my suffering. In the good years, Joseph stores grain beyond counting. When the barns are full, a famine is easy to forget. That's exactly when he gets ready.
screen: `IT IS NOT IN ME.` · `SEVEN OF PLENTY, SEVEN OF FAMINE.` · `STORE A FIFTH IN THE GOOD YEARS.` · `PRISONER TO SECOND IN EGYPT.` · then, large: `STORE IN THE GOOD YEARS.`

segments.voice: Think about what's plentiful in your life right now, money, time, energy, friends, patience, and pick one. Then picture a leaner season that might come, and one small thing you could store up for it now: a few dollars, a phone call to keep a friendship warm, a good night's sleep.
Pharaoh's dreams. Seven fat cows and seven thin: seven years of plenty, seven of famine, and a plan to store grain in the good years.
Your line: store in the good years. Reading the dream was the easy part. Seventy days now: ten whole weeks.
